title: THE WOMEN WHO GAVE GOD THEIR MIRRORS: THE FORGOTTEN SACRIFICE THAT REVEALS WHAT TRUE WORSHIP REALLY COSTS
paragraphs: THE WOMEN WHO GAVE GOD THEIR MIRRORS: THE FORGOTTEN SACRIFICE THAT REVEALS WHAT TRUE WORSHIP REALLY COSTS

They surrendered the bronze that once reflected their faces so it could become part of the place where sinners washed before approaching God. And hidden inside Exodus 38:8 is a truth that could change the way you see your beauty, your brokenness, your worship, and what you are willing to surrender to Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply unsettling about a mirror.
It can show you the face everyone recognizes while concealing the battles nobody knows you are fighting.
It can reveal the wrinkles, the scars, the exhaustion beneath your eyes.
But it cannot reveal the condition of your soul.
It cannot tell you whether your heart is at peace with God.
It cannot measure the weight of your secret regrets.
And it certainly cannot tell you how much you are loved by the One who created you.
Thousands of years ago, in the wilderness, a group of women did something extraordinary.
They brought their bronze mirrors to the construction of God's tabernacle.
And those mirrors became part of something holy.
Not a golden crown.
Not a beautiful ornament.
Not a monument to their generosity.
A basin.
A place where priests would wash.
Read that again.
What had been used to see a human reflection was given for a vessel used in preparation for serving before a holy God.
And if you understand what happened there, you may never look at your own reflection the same way again.
Because sometimes the most meaningful thing you can place before God is something you once believed you could never live without.
Exodus 38:8 records:
"He made the laver of brass, and the foot of it of brass, of the lookingglasses of the women assembling, which assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation." — Exodus 38:8, KJV
One verse.
A handful of words.
An act of generosity that has survived thousands of years.
But behind that verse stands a question that reaches into our lives today.
What are you holding so tightly that you have forgotten it could be used for the glory of God?
To appreciate this moment, we need to understand what Scripture actually says.
The Hebrew text contains the expression:
בְּמַרְאֹת הַצֹּבְאֹת
Bəmarʾōt hatstsōvəʾōt.
It refers to the mirrors of the women who gathered or served in an organized way.
The word marʾōt refers to mirrors, while hatstsōvəʾōt describes the women associated with this gathering or service.

The Hebrew does not tell us their individual names. It does not describe their ages, appearances, marital status, or personal struggles. It does not explicitly say they surrendered their mirrors because they were vain, nor does it tell us what emotions they experienced when giving them.
Those details belong to imagination, not biblical history.
But what the text does tell us is remarkable enough.
Their mirrors were used to make the bronze basin and its stand.
In the ancient world, mirrors were commonly fashioned from polished metal rather than modern glass. Their surfaces reflected an image when carefully maintained.
These women possessed objects that had practical and personal value.
And those objects became material for a sacred purpose.
Imagine the wilderness.
The heat.
The dust.
The tents stretching across the camp.
A people recently delivered from slavery, learning what it meant to belong to the Lord.
For generations, Israel had lived under Pharaoh's power. Now, through God's mighty deliverance, they were being formed into a covenant people.
The tabernacle would stand at the center of their worship, a visible reminder that the God who redeemed them from Egypt intended to dwell among them.
And the construction of that dwelling place required something from the people.
Not because God lacked resources.
Not because the Creator of heaven and earth needed human wealth to survive.
But because He invited His people to participate in the work He had commanded.
Exodus 35:21 says that those whose hearts stirred them and whose spirits made them willing brought offerings for the work of the tabernacle.
And Exodus 35:29 describes the contributions as freewill offerings.
That matters.
Their giving was an act of willing participation, not a payment demanded to purchase God's presence.
There is a world of difference between those two things.
God had already rescued Israel before they contributed materials to the tabernacle.
Their offerings did not buy their redemption.
They responded to the God who had redeemed them.
And there, among the gifts, were the mirrors of women whose names we may never know.
Perhaps you understand something about being unnamed.
You have served faithfully, but someone else received the recognition.
You have prayed for people who never knew you were praying.
You have given quietly when nobody applauded.
You have sacrificed time, money, energy, and comfort while the world continued as though nothing had happened.
Sometimes you wonder whether any of it matters.
Whether heaven notices what earth overlooks.
Whether God remembers the things nobody else bothers to remember.
Then consider these women.
Scripture does not preserve their names.
But it preserves their offering.
Centuries passed.
Kingdoms rose and fell.
Empires disappeared.
Generations were buried.
Yet here we are, still reading about the mirrors they gave.
What was surrendered in obscurity became part of a testimony that outlived them.
Do not underestimate the eternal significance of ordinary faithfulness.
The world may measure your importance by how many people recognize your face.
God sees the heart.
But there is another part of this story that makes the bronze mirrors even more significant.
What did they become?
The basin used by the priests.
Exodus 30:17–21 explains that Aaron and his sons were to wash their hands and feet with water from the basin when entering the tent of meeting or approaching the altar to minister.
This was no ordinary washing station.
It was part of the worship God prescribed for Israel under the old covenant.
The priests were serving a holy God.
And their washing reminded Israel that approaching Him was not something to be treated casually.
The bronze itself did not forgive sins.
The water was not magical.
The basin did not possess independent spiritual power.
The washing belonged to the ceremonial requirements God had established for priestly service.
And that distinction is essential, because the beauty of this passage becomes even greater when we follow the story of Scripture all the way to Jesus Christ.
The tabernacle pointed beyond itself.
Its priesthood, sacrifices, and sacred furnishings belonged to a system that anticipated the greater work God would accomplish through His Son.
Hebrews 9 explains how the old covenant's sanctuary and regulations prepared the way for understanding Christ's superior priestly ministry.
And Hebrews 9:14 asks how much more the blood of Christ will cleanse our consciences from dead works to serve the living God.
Think about that.
The old covenant priest washed his hands and feet before ministering.
But Jesus Christ does something far deeper.
He cleanses what water could never reach.
The conscience burdened by guilt.
The heart poisoned by bitterness.
The soul crushed beneath remembered sin.
The shame you have carried for years.
The darkness you have tried desperately to conceal.
No amount of external washing can remove the guilt of sin before God.
No perfect appearance can make a sinful heart righteous.
No religious performance can replace the saving work of Jesus.
But the blood of Christ is sufficient.
Not because your sin was insignificant.
Because His sacrifice was infinitely greater than anything you could offer.
And suddenly, the story of those bronze mirrors becomes more than an interesting historical detail.
It becomes an opportunity to examine the things we rely upon to tell us who we are.
Some people live before a mirror that constantly tells them they are not beautiful enough.
Others live before the mirror of achievement.
Not successful enough.
Not wealthy enough.
Not respected enough.
Not accomplished enough.
Some are trapped before the mirror of their past.
Every time they look at themselves, they see what they did ten years ago.
The marriage they damaged.
The child they disappointed.
The addiction they concealed.
The promise they broke.
The person they hurt.
The opportunity they wasted.
They keep looking for a different reflection, but the memories refuse to disappear.
And somewhere along the way, they begin to believe their worst moment is their permanent identity.
Maybe that is where you are today.
You smile in public.
You know the Christian vocabulary.
You can say "God is good" even when you feel completely empty.
You can encourage other people while silently wondering whether you have disappointed God beyond repair.
And when the room becomes quiet, the accusations return.
You should have known better.
You have failed too many times.
You are not the person everyone thinks you are.
Why would God still want you?
Listen carefully.
The gospel does not deny the seriousness of your sin.
It does not pretend that rebellion against God is harmless.
It does not call evil good or excuse the damage we have caused.
But it announces something that human shame cannot comprehend.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Not people whose failures were merely cosmetic.
Real sinners.
People who have lied.
People who have betrayed trust.
People who have loved darkness.
People who have tried to hide behind religion.
People who know what it means to stand guilty before a holy God.
The apostle Paul wrote:
"This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief." — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
Paul did not minimize his past.
He knew what he had done.
Yet he also knew that the mercy of Jesus Christ was greater than his former rebellion.
And perhaps you need to hear this today.
Your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die. But His sacrifice is sufficient to save everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
That is not permission to continue in sin.
That is an invitation to come out of hiding.
Because grace is not God pretending you were never guilty.
Grace is God providing salvation through the death and resurrection of His Son.
The Greek New Testament uses a beautiful word for grace:
χάρις — charis.
It speaks of grace, favor, and gift.
And Ephesians 2:8–9 tells us that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works, so that no one may boast.
You cannot buy this grace.
You cannot earn it through donations.
Jesus has already accomplished what no amount of money could accomplish.
The question is whether you will stop trusting yourself and turn to Him.
And here is where the mirrors confront us.
The women of Exodus 38 gave something tangible for the work of God's dwelling place.
But the New Testament calls believers to an even broader response of worship.
Romans 12:1 urges Christians, in view of God's mercies, to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.
Not merely an object.
Not merely a portion of their possessions.
Their very lives.
Their ambitions.
Their relationships.
Their choices.
Their habits.
Their time.
Their resources.
Their obedience.
Everything placed under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And this is where the question becomes uncomfortable.
We may admire the women who gave their mirrors while refusing to surrender the idols hidden inside our own hearts.
We can celebrate their generosity and still cling to our pride.
We can applaud their sacrifice while refusing to forgive someone.
We can speak beautifully about worship while quietly protecting a sin we have no intention of abandoning.
We can say Jesus is Lord while insisting that certain rooms in our lives remain locked.
And the Holy Spirit's work through Scripture exposes that contradiction.
Not to drive repentant sinners into despair.
But to bring us into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice what God promises.
Not merely that He will tolerate us.
Not merely that He will overlook us.
He promises forgiveness and cleansing.
And that cleansing rests upon the righteous work of Jesus Christ.
The same chapter tells us that the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses believers from all sin.
Not some sin.
Not only the respectable sins.
Not only the mistakes that are easy to explain.
All sin.
That does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means the repentant sinner has a Savior whose blood is sufficient.
There is a beautiful scene in John 13 that helps us understand the heart of Christ.
On the night before His crucifixion, Jesus rose from supper, laid aside His outer garments, took a towel, and began washing His disciples' feet.
The Lord of glory stooped before men who did not yet understand the full weight of what was coming.
Peter resisted.
"Lord, dost thou wash my feet?"
And Jesus answered:
"What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter." — John 13:7, KJV
The One who deserved to be served took the posture of a servant.
The One who had no sin washed the feet of sinful men.
And soon, the One who had no guilt would bear the sins of His people upon the cross.
The foot washing was an act of humble love and an example for His disciples. It also took place in the shadow of the greater cleansing His saving work would provide.
Can you see the movement of the biblical story?
In Exodus, priests washed in preparation for sacred service.
In John, the Lord Himself knelt to wash His disciples' feet.
At Calvary, Jesus gave His life to accomplish the redemption that ceremonial washings could never achieve.
And in the resurrection, God declared the victory of His Son over death.
This is why Christianity is not simply a program for becoming a better-looking version of yourself.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Not self-improvement as a substitute for salvation.
New life through the Savior.
The Greek word καινὴ — kainē, used in the expression kainē ktisis in 2 Corinthians 5:17, describes something new.
"If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
Paul is speaking of the new reality of belonging to Christ.
He is not promising that every painful memory will instantly disappear or that Christians will never struggle again.
He is declaring that union with Christ changes a person's standing and life in a way that the old identity cannot define.
And this is where the Gospel Warrior message finds its heartbeat.
Not because Jesus erases history.
Not because He calls our wrongdoing innocent.
Not because He guarantees that every earthly consequence will vanish.
But because the crucified and risen Savior can redeem people whose stories seemed ruined beyond repair.
Think of Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
The man who insisted he would remain faithful even unto death collapsed under the pressure of fear.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter remembered.
Luke 22:62 says he went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine those tears.
The unbearable knowledge that he had denied the very Lord he loved.
The memory of his own confident promises.
The humiliation.
The regret.
The terrible realization that he was not as strong as he believed.
But Peter's story did not end beside that fire of denial.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter and restored him to service, as John 21 records.
The Lord did not pretend the denial had never happened.
He confronted Peter with the question of love and commissioned him to care for His sheep.
The man who had failed was not beyond the reach of Christ's restoring mercy.
And maybe that is the sentence you have been waiting to hear.
Your failure does not have to be the final chapter.
If you are still breathing, do not mistake the invitation to repent for permission to delay repentance.
Come to Christ today.
Not when you have made yourself worthy.
Not when you have repaired your image.
Not when you have convinced everyone that you are spiritually strong.
Come with the truth.
Come with the guilt.
Come with the tears.
Come with the things you have been afraid to confess.
Come to the Savior who said:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." — John 6:37, KJV
And when He saves you, do not return to living as though your worth depends upon the applause of the world.
Your appearance will change.
Your achievements will eventually fade.
Your possessions will pass into other hands.
Even the people who praise you today may forget your name tomorrow.
But what is done in faithful obedience to Christ is not meaningless.
That is one of the enduring lessons we can draw from the women who gave their mirrors.
Their offering was not the foundation of their salvation.
Their gift did not make God indebted to them.
But their willing generosity became part of the work God had commanded.
And today, believers have opportunities to serve Christ through their own resources.
Sometimes that means helping a hungry family.
Sometimes it means supporting a faithful local church.
Sometimes it means providing Bibles, Christian teaching, or discipleship materials to people who cannot afford them.
Sometimes it means giving quietly to someone who has no way to repay you.
But we must keep the order right.
We do not give so that God will love us. We give because He has already shown His love in Christ.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that each person should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That verse protects the beauty of Christian generosity.
Giving must not become a spiritual threat.
But voluntary support of sound gospel work can be a meaningful expression of generosity.
Paul thanked believers who partnered with him in the gospel and supported his ministry, as Philippians 1:5 and 4:15–18 show.
Their gifts were not payments for salvation.
They were expressions of fellowship and love in the work of Christ.
Not out of guilt.
Not because you owe us your money.
But because, if the Lord has used this ministry to encourage you, strengthen your faith, or lead you deeper into Scripture, you may desire to help make that same encouragement available to others.
Every article that points a weary soul back to Jesus matters.
Every biblical resource that helps someone understand the gospel matters.
Every testimony that reminds a struggling believer of Christ's mercy matters.
And if you believe this work should continue and expand, you can become part of sustaining it.
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The gospel is.
And the greatest gift we could ever point you toward is not something you can purchase from a store.
It is the salvation God freely gives through His Son.
Not simply to increase a number.
Not merely to make a page more visible.
Someone may be sitting alone tonight, wondering whether God could ever forgive what they have done.
Someone may be slowly drifting away from the faith.
Someone may be smiling through a marriage that is falling apart.
Someone may be carrying a secret addiction.
Someone may have spent years believing their shame was stronger than the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps a passage of Scripture shared at the right moment will move that person to open a Bible, pray honestly, seek godly counsel, or return to Christ.
You cannot know every burden hidden behind the faces on your screen.
But you can choose to share the truth.
The purpose is not to collect religious information while leaving the heart unchanged.
It is to encourage people to open the Scriptures, know Christ more deeply, grow in sound doctrine, and live in faithful obedience to Him.
Because biblical knowledge should lead us toward worship, humility, love, and holiness.
And before you leave this article, I want to ask you something personal.
Not about your money.
Not about your appearance.
Not about how many people admire you.
What is your mirror?
What has become so important to your identity that the thought of surrendering it to God makes you afraid?
Is it your reputation?
Your need for approval?
Your desire to control every outcome?
Your bitterness toward someone who hurt you?
Your pride in being seen as the strong one?
Your habit of pretending that everything is fine?
Or perhaps it is the reflection of a person you used to be, a reflection you cannot seem to forgive.
Bring it into the light of God's Word.
You do not have to publish your private sins for strangers to read.
You do not have to expose another person's wounds to prove that you are sincere.
But you do need to be honest before God.
And where repentance is necessary, do not settle for emotional words without a changed direction.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust in Jesus Christ.
Seek reconciliation where it is right and possible.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Walk with mature believers who can encourage you in truth.
And remember that genuine spiritual transformation is the work of God's grace, not a performance designed to impress an audience.
You can write "Christ is still healing me" if you are learning to trust His grace through a difficult season.
You can write "No more hiding" if you are ready to walk honestly before God.
You do not have to share details you are not ready to share.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not walking alone.
And if God has brought you through a season of failure into repentance and restoration, consider sharing a testimony that gives glory to Jesus rather than to yourself.
Someone may need to hear that the Savior who restored Peter is still merciful to sinners today.
Now return with me, one final time, to the wilderness.
To the women.
To the mirrors.
To the bronze basin.
There is no recorded speech from those women in Exodus 38:8.
No dramatic farewell to their possessions.
No explanation of how they felt.
No names engraved upon the basin.
Just a brief statement that their mirrors were used in its construction.
And perhaps that is part of what makes their contribution so moving.
They did not need to become the center of the story.
Their gifts became part of something greater than themselves.
The basin stood in the tabernacle where priests washed in obedience to God's command.
And the whole tabernacle system, in its place within redemptive history, directs our attention toward the greater priesthood and finished sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
We should not claim that the women knew every future meaning Christians would later recognize in the tabernacle.
Scripture does not tell us that.
But we can stand on this side of the cross and see how the story of God's dwelling among His people reaches its fulfillment in Christ.
John 1:14 declares:
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
The Greek verb translated "dwelt" is ἐσκήνωσεν — eskēnōsen, meaning that He dwelt or pitched His tent among us.
The language resonates beautifully with the biblical theme of God's presence among His people.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
He entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He bore the judgment sinners deserved.
He died.
He rose again.
And through Him, those who believe are brought near to God.
That is the glory toward which the entire story moves.
Not the bronze.
Not the mirrors.
Not the basin.
Jesus Christ.
The One who sees beyond every outward reflection.
The One before whom every hidden thing is known.
The One who does not excuse sin but offers forgiveness through His own blood.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and gives new life by grace.
The One who can take a life marked by shame and make it a testimony to His mercy.
And maybe tonight, for the first time in a long time, you can stop staring at the person you wish you had been.
You can stop trying to manufacture a spotless image.
You can stop believing that if people discovered your weakness, there would be no hope left for you.
You can turn your eyes toward Jesus Christ.
Not because the mirror has suddenly become beautiful.
But because the Savior is beautiful beyond comparison.
And because His grace is greater than the reflection that has been tormenting you.
The women of Exodus gave their mirrors for the tabernacle.
What will you surrender in obedience to the Lord who gave Himself for you?
Do not answer quickly.
Let the question reach the places where your pride has built walls.
Let Scripture examine what you have been protecting.
Let the gospel remind you that surrender to Christ is not the destruction of your true hope.
It is the beginning of a life no longer ruled by the things that cannot save you.
And when you finally understand that, you may discover something extraordinary.
The most important thing about your life was never the face you saw in the mirror, but the Savior who loved sinners enough to go to the cross.
